'''Herbert Goldstein''' (June 26, 1922 – January 12, 2005) was an American [[physicist]] and the author of the standard graduate textbook ''[[Classical Mechanics (Goldstein book)|Classical Mechanics]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Moulton, E. J.|title=Review: ''Classical Mechanics'' by H. Goldstein|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1952|volume=58|issue=3|pages=396–399|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1952-58-03/S0002-9904-1952-09590-2/S0002-9904-1952-09590-2.pdf|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1952-09590-2|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Life and work ==
Goldstein was well known as the author of the graduate textbook, Classical Mechanics. The book has been a standard text<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Addison |first=Stephen R. |date=July 1, 2002 |title=Book Reviews: Classical Mechanics, 3rd ed. |url=https://pubs.aip.org/ajp/article/70/7/782/1055851/Classical-Mechanics-3rd-ed |journal=American Journal of Physics |language=en |volume=70 |issue=7 |pages=782–783 |doi=10.1119/1.1484149 |issn=0002-9505|url-access=subscription }}</ref> since it first appeared in 1950 and has been translated into nine languages. 
He was widely recognized for his scholarship in classical mechanics and reactor shielding. He received a B.S. from [[City College of New York]] in 1940 and a Ph.D. from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1943. From 1942 to 1946, Goldstein was a staff member of the wartime [[Radiation Laboratory]] at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|M.I.T.]], where he engaged in research on the theory of waveguides and [[Cavity Magnetron|magnetrons]] and on the characteristics of radar echoes. He was an instructor in the physics department at [[Harvard University]] from 1946 to 1949. In 1949–50 he was an [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|AEC]] postdoctoral Fellow at M.I.T., and served as a Visiting Associate Professor of Physics at [[Brandeis University]], 1952–53. From 1950, Goldstein was a senior physicist at Nuclear Development Corporation of America, where he directed theoretical research on the shielding of [[nuclear reactor]]s and on [[neutron]] [[Neutron cross section|cross sections]] of interest for reactor design. Goldstein won the [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award]] in 1962 for his "contributions to reactor physics and to nuclear cross sections, and for his leadership in establishing a rational scientific basis for nuclear shield design".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.apam.columbia.edu/herbert-goldstein-1922-2005|title=Herbert Goldstein, 1922-2005|date=28 April 2017}}</ref>

Goldstein was a professor of nuclear science and engineering at [[Columbia University]]'s [[Fu Foundation School of Engineering and Applied Science]] from 1961 until his death. He received the Great Teacher Award, given by the Society of Columbia Graduates, in 1976. In 1977, he was the recipient of the Distinguished Service Award from the shielding division of the American Nuclear Society.  In 1984, Goldstein was the first to hold the Thomas Alva Edison Professorship at the university. He was professor emeritus at the time of his death.

He was a founding member and served as president of the [[Association of Orthodox Jewish Scientists]].  He was buried in Israel.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Maskewitz, Betty F.|title=Obituary—Herbert Goldstein, Nuclear Scientist—RSICC Friend|journal=RSICC Newsletter|date=February 2005|url=http://www-rsicc.ornl.gov/Newsletters/news.05/news05feb.html#_1_2}}</ref> He was survived by his wife, Channa; his children, Penina, Aaron Meir and Shoshanna; and 10 grandchildren.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.apam.columbia.edu/herbert-goldstein-1922-2005|title=Herbert Goldstein, 1922-2005|date=28 April 2017}}</ref>
